Learn where Euclid DR1 data are stored in the cloud.
Retrieve an image cutout from the cloud.
Retrieve a spectrum from the cloud.

Euclid launched in July 2023 as a European Space Agency (ESA) mission with involvement by NASA.
The primary science goals of Euclid are to better understand the composition and evolution of the dark Universe.
The Euclid mission is providing space-based imaging and spectroscopy as well as supporting ground-based imaging to achieve these primary goals.
These data will be archived by multiple global repositories, including IRSA, where they will support transformational work in many areas of astrophysics.

Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1) comprises about 1900 sq deg of imaging, spectroscopy, and catalogs from the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and from the Euclid Deep Survey (EDS), which covers about 53 sq deg in the three Euclid Deep Fields (North, South, and Fornax).
It follows Quick Release 1 (Q1); all of the DR1 data, including the areas observed in Q1, have been reprocessed with updated pipelines and calibrations.

IRSA maintains copies of the Euclid DR1 data products on the cloud via Amazon Web Services (AWS).
This notebook provides an introduction to accessing Euclid DR1 data from the cloud.

children.value: column that gives us the location info of the image files we are interested in. So let’s extract the S3 bucket file path from it:

def get_s3_fpath(cloud_access):
    cloud_info = json.loads(cloud_access) # converts str to dict
    bucket_name = cloud_info['aws']['bucket_name']
    key = cloud_info['aws']['key']

    return f'{bucket_name}/{key}'
Let’s also extract filter names to use when displaying the images:

def get_filter_name(instrument, bandpass):
    return f'{instrument}_{bandpass}' if instrument!=bandpass else instrument
These image files are very big (~1.4GB), so we use astropy’s lazy-loading capability of FITS for better performance. (See
Obtaining subsets from cloud-hosted FITS files

cutouts = []
filters = []

for row in euclid_sci_img_tbl:
    s3_fpath = get_s3_fpath(row['cloud_access'])
    filter_name = get_filter_name(row['instrument_name'], row['energy_bandpassname'])

    with fits.open(f's3://{s3_fpath}', fsspec_kwargs={"anon": True}) as hdul:
        print(f'Retrieving cutout for {filter_name} ...')
        cutout = Cutout2D(hdul[0].section,
                          position=coord,
                          size=cutout_size,
                          wcs=WCS(hdul[0].header))
        cutouts.append(cutout)
        filters.append(filter_name)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(4 * 2, 4 * 2), subplot_kw={'projection': cutouts[0].wcs})

for idx, ax in enumerate(axes.flat):
    norm = ImageNormalize(cutouts[idx].data, interval=PercentileInterval(99), stretch=AsinhStretch())
    ax.imshow(cutouts[idx].data, cmap='gray', origin='lower', norm=norm)
    ax.set_xlabel('RA')
    ax.set_ylabel('Dec')
    ax.text(0.95, 0.05, filters[idx], color='white', fontsize=14, transform=ax.transAxes, va='bottom', ha='right')

plt.tight_layout()

column flags flux bins that should not be used; bins with an odd

value or a value of 64 or more are flagged.
These include the low-flux bins at both ends of the wavelength range, so we set the y-axis range from the unflagged bins to show the spectrum in more detail.

good = (spec_tbl['MASK'] % 2 == 0) & (spec_tbl['MASK'] < 64)
good_signal = spec_tbl['SIGNAL'][good]
margin = 0.05 * (good_signal.max() - good_signal.min())

# In DR1, the flux scale factor (the FSCALE header keyword) is already included in the unit of the SIGNAL column,
# so we plot the signal as is and label the axis with that unit.
plt.plot(spec_tbl['WAVELENGTH'], spec_tbl['SIGNAL'])
plt.ylim(good_signal.min() - margin, good_signal.max() + margin)
plt.xlabel(spec_tbl['WAVELENGTH'].unit.to_string('latex_inline'))
plt.ylabel(spec_tbl['SIGNAL'].unit.to_string('latex_inline'))
